Discussion ### 4.1 What the ankle result does and does not say about the variable clinicians watch Both the variable clinicians observe and the variable recent instrumented studies analyse is foot or ankle position at contact [4, 5].
The result here is narrower than "the ankle is uninformative at contact", and an earlier draft of this manuscript made that broader claim before withdrawing it.

The finding is also not an explanation. §3.7 shows that in this system a single-muscle lesion displaces joints its muscle does not cross, so the joint at which a difference appears does not identify the muscle responsible, and no mechanism for the knee's behaviour was established. ### 4.2 The one adult-stroke attempt does not support this model, and says so at the relevant muscle The comparison that matters is the gastrocnemius column of Cawood and Mashola [7], because gastrocnemius is one of the two muscles lesioned here.
The only patient dataset that has measured exactly that relationship does not find it.

**The study therefore cannot distinguish "no relationship" from "a relationship of the size it observed", and its null is uninformative rather than adverse.** It is also a feasibility pilot in a subacute cohort — median 4.0 months since stroke, when tone is still evolving — in which 9 of 12 had any gastrocnemius tone, graded on the Modified Tardieu 0–4 muscle-reaction scale against 2D video.
Tibialis anterior is the muscle this study lesions by *weakening*, not by adding tone, so the two results concern different perturbations of the same muscle and cannot be compared directly.

It is nonetheless the second independent indication in this manuscript — with the patient dataset of Limitation 5 — that the dorsiflexor side of the ankle, not the plantarflexor side, is what visibly moves the knee in real hemiparetic gait.

This generates the specific test: in a mixed cohort, a model containing both a plantarflexor spasticity term and a dorsiflexor term should recover at contact what single-variable correlation cannot — and should be powered as a regression against the between-patient spread above; it is not a two-group design, since §4.4 notes that pure-lesion groups could not be recruited.
It is tempting to argue that Cawood et al. chose their window post hoc while this work had an a priori reason to prefer contact.

**That argument is not available here**: our contact-versus-stance comparison was itself chosen after observing a disagreement between two ankle results (Limitation 1). ### 4.3 Relation to the hamstring precedent Knee flexion at contact already indexes graded spasticity of a muscle that crosses the knee directly [6].

That makes this cross-joint propagation rather than direct action — and §3.7 shows the propagation does not follow muscle attachment anatomy in this system. ### 4.4 What this offers, and what it would take For a clinician the practical content is narrow but specific: at foot contact, expect the knee to move toward flexion with plantarflexor spastic severity.

Because the model cannot walk with severe weakness, whether the axis becomes readable at clinically typical weakness depth is untested rather than excluded, and extending it is the second experiment this work calls for.

**The grading result, not the discrimination, is the part with a route to the clinic.** No patient is purely spastic or purely weak, so a discriminator between *pure* lesions answers a question the clinic does not face — and §3.3 shows directly that a single reading cannot recover the mixture.

⚠ **It is not, however, the readout the clinic needs.** §1.1 locates the unmet question as apportionment — how much of the deviation each component contributes, and whether the dorsiflexors will work once the antagonist is silenced — and a readout that cannot report the weakness component does not answer it.
What the grading result offers is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one: if the gradient does not exist in patients, nothing downstream is worth attempting.

In the other direction, stance-phase knee hyperextension after stroke is conventionally attributed to plantarflexor overactivity or shortening, and both plantarflexor spasticity [8] and plantarflexor weakness [17] are reported to accompany it, so an extended knee does not isolate the dorsiflexor either.

**The obvious within-patient design carries an unresolved risk.** Measuring knee angle at contact before and after a diagnostic nerve block in the same limb would cancel session-level measurement error, which §3.5 identifies as the main obstacle.

But a block is acute plantarflexor paresis with no opportunity for motor re-optimisation, and a frozen-controller probe (Limitation 9) found weakness moving the knee in the same direction as spasticity.
That probe's cells do not walk and cannot be compared with the main result, so this is a risk rather than a refutation — but it should be resolved in simulation before a patient is recruited.

Two modelling steps should run alongside it: a contracture arm at the one-parameter cost Ong et al. established [10], without which the readout cannot be attributed to reflex overactivity rather than plantarflexor shortness of any origin; and a model that reaches the severity these patients present with.

A between-group patient study is not licensed — and could not be recruited as designed, because the cohort that motivates the question carries both components at group level — dorsiflexor *and* plantarflexor strength are each significantly reduced in the spastic group [4], although that paper reports no per-limb co-occurrence count — so there are no dependable pure-spasticity and pure-weakness groups to enrol. --- ### 4.5 Limitations 1.

**The analysed severity window is itself post-observation.** The title, abstract and primary claim are stated over KV 0.050–0.120; its lower edge is where the claim stops holding, since at KV 0.0125 and 0.025 the knee arms interleave (§3.2).

**The arms are confounded with simulation survival.** Run within the spastic arm's own 8 s end-time spread, the within-dose duration control gives a mean of 36% of the effect but ranges from **−182% to +96%** across the five families, so it **neither retires nor confirms** the confound (§3.2).
An earlier revision quoted the four-family range −14% to +96%, which understates the control's instability and so ran in this study's favour.

**Two further facts about what the hyperreflexia arm's gait is must be stated.** First, its **medio-lateral excursion is divergent inside the measurement window**: lateral drift is +0.051 m/cycle against the control arm's +0.0005, monotone in every spastic cell of every rung, and lateral femur range runs 0.102–0.205 m against control's 0.019 m — 5.4× to 10.9×, dose-monotone.

The sagittal knee channel was checked separately and is stationary within the window (§2.4 rule 3), so the reported knee mean is not itself an average over a divergence; but **the arm is losing lateral balance while it is being measured, and Gate G does not test for that**.
Second, the same fact is why Limitation 9 sets the frozen-controller probe aside; that reasoning is available only if these cells are accepted as gait, and they are laterally divergent too.

**The separation window's lower edge and the model's survival edge are the same edge.** At KV 0.0125 and 0.025 — the two gains at which no cell falls, every seed reaching 20 s — knee angle at contact is −6.18° and −6.81°, inside the weakness band; at KV 0.050, the lowest gain at which the arms separate, five of six cells fall.
Nothing was simulated between 0.025 and 0.050, a factor of two, so the coincidence is unlocalised and this manuscript cannot say which of the two boundaries the separation follows. 3.
The objection is testable here without new simulation, because the confounder is measured on the same cells: if the knee merely followed the ankle, the knee ordering would track the ankle ordering.

Across the 30 hyperreflexia × weakness family pairs the knee difference keeps one sign, the ankle difference does not, and in **11 of the 30 pairs the hyperreflexia limb's ankle is *less* plantarflexed than the weakness limb's — by up to 1.52°, and in every case by more than the 0.586° sham floor — while its knee is 2.99–5.44° more flexed**.

Ankle position at contact cannot produce that. (Thirteen pairs falsify mediation on sign alone; two are dropped because their ankle differences, +0.015° and +0.370°, fall below the artefact floor this manuscript applies to its own positive claims.) Those 11 pairs are the low-gain rungs KV 0.050 and 0.070, at which the hyperreflexia ankle sits *above* the entire weakness band — separated from it in the direction opposite to the one mediation needs, rather than interleaved with it.

What this licenses is narrow: the knee separation is not wholly a passive consequence of ankle position, and over the interleaving range it cannot be one at all — not that ankle position plays no part at high gain.

In an earlier phase of this project one registration was edited after its result was produced, together with its analysis script and regenerated outputs, and the hash sidecars were re-baselined — so hash verification cannot detect that breach and the revision the run executed under is not recoverable.

**Simulation only, and the one real-patient dataset examined is half against us.** A public dataset of 50 stroke survivors cannot test this discrimination — no spasticity or strength scale, no soleus channel, no MVC normalisation, no speed — but on the one relation it addresses it is not neutral.
**The weakness arm does not reproduce steppage.** Clinically, dorsiflexor weakness provokes increased hip and knee flexion in swing to clear the toe.
**Both lesions have a severity ceiling, and the arms are not comparable in dose.** The model walks to ×0.70 weakness and KV 0.120; beyond, it falls.
This ceiling, not a demonstrated property of the endpoint, is also why the weakness axis of §3.3 is shallow; with the cells that exist the two cannot be separated. 8.
Lesion type is additionally confounded with optimisation round, though §3.2 shows the contrast holding within round 151 alone, as a subset re-analysis.

Family-level confidence intervals are reported in §3.1, where the earlier equivalence test for the ankle at contact is also withdrawn; no confidence intervals are attached to the per-cycle, video or sub-phase quantities. 9.

**The discrimination may depend on re-optimisation, and this design cannot settle whether it does.** A probe with the controller frozen rather than re-optimised found an isolated soleus-*weakness* condition displacing the knee toward flexion, in the same direction as the spastic arm.

⚠ That probe cannot be compared with §3.1: **every lesioned arm in it fails Gate G**, dying in 3–5 s on one to two gait cycles against a five-cycle bar, and its own deposit records that none of its numbers may be placed beside a Gate-G value, since doing so compares a steady walk against a fall.

**The most relevant patient comparison is uninformative rather than adverse, and this manuscript has misread it three times.** Gastrocnemius tone is unrelated to knee angle at every stance phase in [7] (ρ = 0.362, p = 0.22 at initial contact), against this model's central dose prediction (§4.2), but at n = 12 that null could not have detected anything below ρ = 0.79.

Ankle angle at the same instant does not: it grades plantarflexor gain just as strongly, but over that identical range its ladder passes through the weakness band, so the sign of the between-arm contrast flips and the two lesions read as opposite, indistinguishable or aligned depending on severity.

**The robust finding is the sign reversal, not its magnitude.** The difference is 5.28° pooled across doses, −5.593° (95% CI [−7.380, −3.806]) at the family level, and **4.087° within round 151**, which removes the round and chaining confounds but is not dose-matched — on this project's registered force-dose metric the matched pairing gives 3.420° (§3.2).

The quantity that must clear the pipeline's noise is not the between-arm difference but the smallest single-family displacement from control, which is +0.908° against a largest measured artefact of 0.586° — a margin of 1.5×, the thinnest point in the argument.

Cell-level disjointness from control does not repair that margin — the nearest control-to-arm cell gap is 0.387°, two thirds of one artefact unit — which is why the primary claim here is stated arm-versus-arm and not against control.
What none of them can do is produce a *sign reversal*: they are unsigned procedural displacements, and dose asymmetry can inflate an excursion but cannot flip its direction.

**The largest confound is survival and it is not resolved.** All 23 hyperreflexia cells fall and all 42 other cells do not; the within-dose duration control run inside the spastic arm gives a mean of 36% of the effect across four families, or −7% across five, and ranges from −182% to +96%, so it is too imprecise to settle the question.
Three of its five family slopes are positive and would shrink the difference rather than create it; the fourth is negative and would enlarge it, so the confound is not one-directional either.

The family permutation p = 0.0022 should also be read carefully: 1/462 is the smallest value the design can return, and the labels being permuted are confounded with survival and round, so the test establishes that these lineages separate — not that lesion type is why.

**And it does not currently transfer.** The effect is below the threshold for declaring change in one patient; the model's gait is milder than the target population's and reproduces neither steppage nor the increased swing knee flexion that clears the toe; the simulated severity does not reach the patients who receive diagnostic blocks; a 50-patient dataset supports the weakness arm while running against the hyperreflexia arm, and the one study to grade plantarflexor tone against knee angle was powered only for ρ ≥ 0.79, so its null neither supports nor refutes the gradient — but it is the only patient test of the relation this paper's grading claim rests on, and it did not find it.
This grades one lesion within a *known* weakness background; it does not recover the mixture, and §3.3 shows a single reading cannot.

It is closer to what a mixed population would need than a discriminator between pure lesions, but it is calibrated to no clinical scale, the only patient test of the relation found nothing, and it does not answer the apportionment question §1.1 identifies as the clinical one.
